extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and students of logic/scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for forming, testing, and generalizing scientific hypotheses and inductive inferences; covers when different experimental/inductive methods apply, limits of explanation, and probabilistic reasoning. Emphasizes criteria for legitimate hypothesis, vera causa, and the proper use of experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The law that causes composing together produce corresponding composed effects (duplication of causes will generally duplicate effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill defends this law against apparent exceptions (e.g., two sparks vs one, double doses of medicine) by noting that apparent failures arise from attending to remote instead of immediate effects. Examples: two men could raise a gun to angle twice as quickly; two sparks set two sets of particles into the state that makes them explode. Doubling collocation in different time/place does double the effect. Where a collocation once obtained suffices to produce the maximal effect at that time/place, doubling may not increase the observed effect but still fulfills the law when immediate effects are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish immediate from remote effects when evaluating cause duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions to cause-composition often result from observing remote effects while the immediate (duplicated) effect exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a certain collocation (e.g. a particular configuration) is all that is required to produce the effect at a given time/place, duplicating that collocation need not double the observed effect; but the immediate effect (the collocation) is still doubled. Apply this distinction when interpreting experiments like multiple guns, multiple sparks, or medicine doses (aperients vs narcotics and their remote consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude effects produced by the means of producing the antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the consequent might have been generated, not by the antecedent itself, but by the means used to produce the antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the means are under our power, we can often investigate whether they could be the true cause. This requires considering and testing the operations employed to bring about the antecedent (e.g., clearing clouds as a 'natural experiment' that may have independent effects on deposition of dew).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Methods: Agreement, Difference, and Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the inductive method appropriate to the case: Methods of Agreement and Difference suit cases with controlled contrasts; Concomitant Variations is useful when a cause happens to vary alone and the effect varies with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concomitant Variations can single out influencing causes by noting antecedents whose variation is followed by variation in the effect (examples: appetite with cold, tidal influence of sun/moon, nitrogen elimination with exercise). But if many causes vary or none predominate, tracing relations sufficient to assign real shares to individual causes is often impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of Concomitant Variations with multiple influencing causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When many influencing causes act and none predominates, or when several are continually changing, Concomitant Variations rarely suffices to determine each cause's share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about attributing quantitative shares to individual causes under complex, multivariate conditions; other methods or deductions may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiment for elementary laws; use deduction for complex combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and experiment are the ultimate basis of all knowledge for elementary laws of life and nature; but in complex combinations experimental methods are often illusory and deductive investigation must be invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nerve functions discovered by experiments on animals; but in complex systems (e.g., political or economic phenomena) rely more on deductive reasoning to disentangle complexities that experimental repetition can't isolate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of a scientific hypothesis: deduce consequences and compare with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is legitimate if one can deduce its consequences and subject those consequences to observation or experiment to disprove or corroborate the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cites Broussais (local origin of certain fevers), Gilbert (earth as magnet), and speculative examples (brain as voltaic pile, Gall's localization) as legitimate when they enable testable deductions. Even if ultimately false, such hypotheses can be justified if they facilitate refutation or further inquiry. Hypotheses must therefore be framed so that their consequences are observable and comparable with facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa requirement (cause capable of producing like effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate causal hypothesis should be of a vera causa — demonstrably capable of producing effects of the same kind as those attributed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill praises Darwin's natural selection as an example: it is a vera causa because it has been shown to be capable of producing effects of the kind ascribed (though degree remains a question). Hypotheses must address the question of possibility (can the proposed cause produce the observed phenomena?) not merely similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards for hypothesis vs induction
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is not bound by the rules of Induction (which concern proof); it is subject to the rules of Hypothesis (which govern conjecture and investigatory fruitfulness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes that proposing a hypothesis does not require it to be proved inductively at the outset; what matters is that it is testable, fruitful for inquiry, and not obviously impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of cause requires production under the same law
rubrics_metrics.description: To generalize disparate phenomena into one cause is scientifically legitimate only if the cause can be shown to produce them according to the same law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that while phenomena may be grouped under a 'single agency' (e.g., attraction), success of such generalization depends on whether the cause produces effects under the same law; if the manner of production differs widely, asserting unity is merely a nominal generalization that adds no explanatory advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to explanation: do not merge distinct forces without common law
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if two forces share a feature (e.g., attraction), they should not be merged into one explanatory law unless they conform to the same operative law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: gravity vs cohesion — both attractive, but differ in manner (inverse square vs short-range substance-specific behavior); merging them would be illusory and not simplify understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical support for hypotheses must be weighed cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies (e.g., light's travel/time/interception analogous to mechanical undulations) can support hypotheses but do not prove identity of underlying mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The undulatory theory of light gains support from such analogies, but we must not assume mechanical motion is the only possible explanation simply from analogies; hypotheses should remain open to alternative interpretations and further empirical test.

rubrics_metrics.name: First instance establishes possibility; frequency indexes cause strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The first observed instance of a phenomenon primarily shows its possibility (i.e., existence of an adequate cause); subsequent instances matter as indices to the intensity or invariability of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill explains why the first instance often adds more to our probability judgment than any single subsequent instance: it shows the event is possible. Later repetitions increase confidence by indicating control and invariability of the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer future occurrence solely from past frequency without reference to causes
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not conclude straight from past occurrences to future probability without considering the underlying cause; if the causes change, past frequency may not predict future events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequency-based calculations (comparing cases where event occurs vs not) underlie insurance and practical chance estimates, but they fail when intervening changes in causal collocations occur. Always assess stability of causal conditions before projecting probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerating possibilities for probabilistic calculation requires empirical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculations of chances break down when there is no data or principled way to enumerate all relevant possibilities; without empirical frequencies or a justified listing of possibilities, probability assignments are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill contrasts the simple colored-balls model (where we define possibilities) with natural cases where the 'space' of possibilities (e.g., all colors) is not well-defined and depends on what standard of distinction (common eye vs painter's eye) is used. Probability requires either empirical frequency data or a principled, defensible definition of the sample space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate estimator for central tendency in induction (least squares principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inductive determinations of invariable elements, the most probable estimate is that in which the sum of the squares of individual deviations is the least possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes that the mean (in the inductive sense) is not always the arithmetic average when deviations are asymmetric; use the least-squares principle (minimize sum of squares) to determine the most probable central value, as explained by Herschel and Laplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural experiments often have limited value without corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural 'experiments' (where nature approximates human experiment) are of limited value if the means by which the natural experiment occurs are complex or imperfectly understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nature 'clearing off a canopy of clouds' is of little value unless we understand the process and can rule out independent effects of the means on the phenomenon (dew deposition). Natural experiments can corroborate conclusions but rarely suffice alone when the means are unanalyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of nature is a conditional assumption and acquired idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions of physical science are conditional on the uniformity of nature; belief in universal uniformity is not intuitive but results from extended inductive study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that uniformity is sufficiently proved for practical purposes by experience, but recognizes philosophical challenges (e.g., claims that transcendental proof is required). For scientific conduct, conditional acceptance of uniformity provides adequate certainty for guidance of action.
